newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - GAN'S CIC increases profits by 36 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - GAN'S CIC increases profits by 36 pct.

text.p: Regional French bank Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) revealed a 36 percent increase in 1996 profit on Tuesday and said it expected to be privatised this year after a first attempt was scrapped last autumn.

CIC, a subsidiary of the loss-making state insurer Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN), said net attributable profit rose 36 percent to 847 million francs ($148.9 million) in 1996 from 625 million a year earlier.

CIC Chairman Philippe Pontet, who took over when predecessor Bernard Yoncourt was removed after angering the Finance Ministry during the first privatisation attempt, said he expected a marked rise in profit this year, which would help secure a sell-off.

He said the plan was still to privatise CIC via a trade sale rather than a public share offer and that the group, comprising 11 regional banks with strong local ties to small and medium sized businesses, would not be sold off in pieces.
"We're still working with the scenario of seeking a suitor via a trade sale...with GAN as the second reference shareholder," Pontet said in a salesman-style presentation of 1996 results.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis scrapped a first attempt to sell off 67 percent of CIC last November after getting just one eligible offer in a tender -- from Banque Nationale de Paris. An offer from Societe Generale was ruled out by the Privatisation Commission.
Yoncourt's televised criticism of how the privatisation was shaping up cost him his job. The government then fired the head of CIC parent GAN, Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, in the wake of the flop.

"When I hear that the state has nothing but difficult things to privatise, it's certainly not the case for CIC," he told a news conference. "This year should register a new and marked progression in results," he added.
CIC's net banking income rose 3.4 percent to 17.13 billion francs from 16.56 billion, while operating costs climbed 1.7 percent to 13.11 billion francs.
Pontet said the group's return on equity, a key measure for comparing bank performance, came in at 6.3 percent.
"The aim is to achieve 10 percent as soon as possible," he said while declining to forecast how fast that might happen.

While Pontet's punchy style in presenting the 1996 results contrasted strongly with that of his more dead-pan predecessor, he appeared to be sticking by most of the conditions which the Finance Ministry had imposed during the first sale tender.

He stressed that the banking group's federal structure had to be preserved, that the chairman of its constituent regional banks had agreed that privatisation at the regional level was not on the cards and that CIC's commercial ties with GAN should be seen as a help rather than a hindrance.
CIC recently renewed a 10-year "bancassurance" contract for the sale of GAN life assurance through the CIC network and Pontet emphasised that GAN should remain a key ally after sell-off.
"We are seeking a majority, quality shareholder as our main shareholder, with GAN the second biggest shareholder."

Arthuis also plans to privatise GAN this year once he has cleaned up a balance sheet gutted by losses in the collapsed property market and price-cutting in some insurance businesses, but timing and terms of both sell-offs have yet to be set. ($ = 5.689 French Francs)
